items.title: Maria Schneider interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001
items.q: there’s a lot of great composers that weren’t really discovered in their lifetime that much, the Charles Ives and people who went a great portion of their life being really unrecognized

ctx.x: Yeah. It’s not your job. Wow. I’ll shorten this one up, but it says, “love of music doesn’t always manifest itself in the wish to make money as a musician. Having a monstrous career is not a marking stick for being successful.” That’s a heavy statement.

Yeah, there’s a lot of great composers that weren’t really discovered in their lifetime that much, the Charles Ives and people who went a great portion of their life being really unrecognized yet were strong in developing what they did. It didn’t really change anything for them. I mean easy to say, because I’ve been lucky that way. But I have to say I didn’t expect to have the career that I have. I actually didn’t even set out to do it. I kind of expected, I honestly, people laugh and they think that I’m joking,…

to feel like I have to do this. And I always wanted to do what I’m doing because I want to. I don’t, you know if I decided I didn’t want to write music — I doubt it would happen but it could — that if I wanted to quit and just do something else, say I just suddenly got interested in something else creatively, I would just do that. In college I almost switched majors to astrophysics.
